description:
Шестеро странных

В ядре нейтронной звезды, за порогом деконфайнмента, обитали шесть странных кварков — не по характеру, а по аромату. А снаружи, за десятки световых лет, кто-то писал статью с осторожной фразой: «not yet excluded by observation» — и в этом было куда больше правды, чем в любой из историй.
summary:
TUMAR is a rapid health self-assessment system for astronauts on long missions, where Earth-based doctors cannot respond instantly.

We developed three connected parts. The first is a research paper that answers the challenge's core question: which health indicators matter most? We mapped NASA's five spaceflight hazards to 15 candidate indicators and scored each on five criteria. Ten became core, including cabin CO₂, radiation, sleep, resting heart rate, SpO₂ and a 3-minute reaction-time test. Cabin conditions are checked against NASA limits, and body signals are compared with each astronaut's own 14-day baseline, because group averages hide individual differences. Every reading becomes a green, yellow or red status with a clear action.

The second part is a web prototype built on this research. It shows a clickable body figure with system statuses and recommendations, and runs mostly on synthetic data.

The third part is hardware: our engineers built wristband prototypes with a MAX30102 sensor that stream live heart rate and SpO₂ to the website over local Wi-Fi.

TUMAR matters because it gives the crew one clear answer and one next step without waiting for Earth.
details:
What it does and how it works

TUMAR is a crew health twin for deep-space missions. It helps astronauts answer one question fast: is everything all right, and if not, what should I do next? The project has three connected parts: a research paper, a web prototype, and two linked wristbands with a mobile app.

The research paper decides what to measure. We mapped NASA's five spaceflight hazards to 15 candidate health indicators and scored each on five criteria: link to a hazard, measurability on board, early-warning value, actionability and speed. Ten indicators became core: cabin CO2, inspired O2, cabin temperature and humidity, radiation, sleep, exercise, resting heart rate, skin temperature, SpO2 and a 3-minute reaction-time test. Three are supporting and two were excluded. The paper also defines how readings become a decision. Cabin conditions and SpO2 are checked against fixed limits, mostly from NASA standards. Body signals are compared with each astronaut's own baseline from the previous 14 days: a reading two standard deviations away on two consecutive days turns yellow, and three turns red. Each status comes with a specific action.

The web prototype puts this logic into practice. Its main screen shows a clickable human figure. The astronaut selects a body system and sees its status, trend and recommendation. Other sections link crew health to the task schedule, show space weather from public NASA and NOAA feeds, compare the whole crew, plot trends and run a quick check-up. Four scenarios demonstrate the logic: nominal flight, CO2 scrubber failure, solar storm and onboard infection.

The wristbands connect the system to the body. They are linked with each other, with the website and with a mobile app. The main wristband is our own device, built from scratch. It measures heart rate and blood oxygen (SpO2) with a skin sensor and shows heart rate, SpO2, a live pulse wave and the connection status on its screen. Nine RGB LEDs along the edge show status and flash with the pulse. Data go to the website over the local network, and firmware updates arrive over the air, so the wristband never has to be opened. The second wristband shows the partner's live pulse and receives SOS alarms.

SOS between crewmates: an astronaut presses the SOS button on their wristband, and it calls the other astronauts on board over the local network. Their wristbands sound the buzzer and show who needs help. The partner presses their button to answer "on my way", the alarm stops, and the caller gets a confirmation. The same SOS opens a call-for-help window on the website.

Benefits

The astronaut gets one clear status and one next step instead of a wall of numbers. Personal baselines catch changes that a single group norm would miss or falsely flag. All calculations run on board, so no contact with Earth is needed. The wristbands make monitoring continuous and hands-free, and SOS lets crewmates help each other in seconds, even when ground support is minutes away.

Intended impact

On missions to the Moon or Mars, crews will have to notice health problems themselves. TUMAR aims to help them catch problems early, before symptoms appear, act with confidence, and call each other for help instantly. The same approach could help people in remote or isolated places on Earth, such as polar stations, ships or remote expeditions.

Tools and technologies

- Research: NASA Human Research Program resources (5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight, Risks of Human Spaceflight, Ongoing HRP Research), NASA-STD-3001, NASA OCHMO technical briefs, Canadian Space Agency resources and peer-reviewed spaceflight studies.
- Software: a web application deployed on Vercel, with space-weather data from NASA DONKI and NOAA, and a mobile app connected to the wristbands.
- Hardware, main wristband: ESP-12F Wi-Fi module with over-the-air (OTA) firmware updates, MAX30102 optical heart rate and SpO2 sensor, 0.96" OLED display, 9 addressable RGB LEDs, two buttons (one for SOS), buzzer with a transistor driver, Li-ion battery with an AP2112K 3.3 V regulator and a 3D-printed case worn on a strap like a watch.
- Hardware, second wristband: ESP32-C3 with a small OLED screen.
- PCB manufacturing: we drew the schematic and the board in KiCad, printed the layout, transferred the toner onto copper-clad board, etched it and soldered every part by hand.

Creativity

Instead of building a dashboard of everything, we first asked which indicators are worth measuring and scored them openly. We combined fixed safety limits for the environment with personal baselines for the body, and joined crew health, cabin conditions, space weather and the mission schedule in one interface with a clickable body figure. We designed and etched our own wristband board rather than only using a ready-made kit, and added crew-to-crew SOS, so the system supports not only self-assessment but also mutual help.

Factors we considered

- what can realistically be measured on board without a lab;
- false alarms versus missed problems;
- the first days of adaptation to weightlessness;
- missing data, which is shown as "no data" rather than green;
- that astronauts are not doctors, so the tool gives actions, not diagnoses;
- that the wristband must be updatable without opening it and must work over a local network without Earth;
- that in an emergency a crewmate is the fastest help.

We were also honest about limits. The website runs mostly on synthetic data with simplified parameters, live data come only from the wristbands (heart rate and SpO2), and the rules still need validation. As next steps, we proposed a synthetic experiment with 500 virtual astronauts, testing on real data and review by flight surgeons.
